name: Alvarado score

summary: The alvarado score calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports alvarado score immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer. It suits an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Alvarado score calculator work?
sections.html:
The Alvarado score calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports alvarado score in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the body temperature and the white blood count).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A single on/off switch — tick it for “Right lower quadrant tenderness (Pain in the right lower quadrant during palpation.)”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Rebound tenderness (Presence of pain upon removal of pressure on the abdominal wall.)”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as above 99.1 °F (37.3 °C) and within normal limits. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Migration of pain (Epigastric pain migrating to the right lower quadrant of the abdomen.)”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Anorexia”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Nausea”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as 10,000/µL and more and no leukocytosis. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Left shift (Increased number of immature leukocytes in the peripheral blood, particularly neutrophil band cells.)”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.

8 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Alvarado score calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Alvarado score=(anorexia + body temperature + left shift + white blood count + migration of pain + nausea + rebound + right tenderness)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — Body temperature set to Above 99.1 °F (37.3 °C) and White blood count set to 10,000/µL and more — it reports Alvarado score = 2.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Alvarado score = 2 should be roughly the size you expected from Body temperature set to Above 99.1 °F (37.3 °C) and White blood count set to 10,000/µL and more.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Alvarado score calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Alvarado score calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns alvarado score. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Alvarado score calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 8 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (8 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Alvarado score = 2. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Alvarado score calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
